title: The sabbath without evening (13.35–13.36)
hook: a refrain you can hear coming, then silence: Genesis gives the seventh day no evening, and Augustine ends his book there
tomorrow: why does a book called Confessions open with praise, not sin?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two readers, one verse, and Augustine's surprise: more than one reading can be true, if it's true and fits love. The line was in charity.

Some songs have a refrain you can feel coming before it lands; by the third time, you're singing it. The first chapter of Genesis has one. In the Douay-Rheims: "and there was evening and morning one day." Then the second day, evening and morning. The third. A beat, like a clock ticking through creation. Six times. Then the seventh day comes, God rests, and the beat just doesn't arrive. No evening. No morning. Silence where the refrain should be. Augustine heard that silence, and he ended the Confessions inside it.
screen: `A REFRAIN YOU FEEL COMING.` → `EVENING AND MORNING, SIX TIMES.` → `DAY SEVEN: SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's how he reads it. Everything God made is very good, Augustine says, and still it passes; those days had a morning and an evening. But the seventh day has no evening, because God made it holy to last. So his last prayer in the book asks for peace: in the Pusey translation, "the peace of the Sabbath, which hath no evening." Then he turns it toward us. God rested after his works, he says, so that after ours, which are good only by God's gift, we too may rest in God, in the sabbath of eternal life. Listen to how far that reaches back. On the first page, the heart was restless until it rests in God. On the last, the rest arrives, and it's a day with no sunset, nothing ticking toward the end. The whole life story sits between those two lines. That's something to tell a friend tonight: the Confessions doesn't end on Augustine at all. It ends on Genesis, and on a rest that has no evening.
screen: `GOOD THINGS STILL PASS.` · `THE PEACE THAT HATH NO EVENING.` · `AFTER OUR WORKS, REST IN GOD.` · `RESTLESS ON PAGE ONE, AT REST AT THE END.` · then, large: `A SABBATH WITHOUT EVENING.`

segments.voice: Let your hands fall open on your lap, palms up, and let your shoulders drop as if today's work were already finished. Stay like that, unhurried, the way a day rests when no evening is coming to end it.
The sabbath without evening. Augustine's last picture: God's rest on the seventh day, a rest in God that never ends.
Keep this one: a sabbath without evening, the rest the restless heart was looking for all along. Sleep well.

notes: Genesis 1:5 and Confessions 13.35 (Pusey) quoted; confirm wording.
'Six times': Genesis 1 repeats the evening-and-morning refrain for days one through six (1:5, 8, 13, 19, 23, 31) and not for the seventh day (2:2–3). Confirm the count.
13.36: the seventh day has no evening because God sanctified it to abide; after our works, good by his gift, we rest in him in the sabbath of eternal life. Paraphrased; confirm.
Latin 'pacem quietis, pacem sabbati, pacem sine vespera' (13.35.50); game uses the last three words. Confirm.
Fork mentions a funeral and the prayer 'eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord' (described, not quoted from a translation). Gentle; no scene of death is told.
